chapters.title: Chapter 1: Why Forex Charts Read Differently From Stock Charts

lessons.title: Candlesticks on Currency Pairs: Doji, Pin Bars and Engulfing Patterns Around Session Opens

children.text: Rohit trades USD/INR futures on NSE and has noticed something odd. Roughly once a week, the very first five-minute candle after the 9:00 am open has a long lower wick, a classic hammer shape, and he has started buying it every time expecting a reversal. Some days it works beautifully. Other days price keeps falling straight through his stop-loss within the hour. Rohit is not reading the candle wrong. He is reading it without asking the one question that matters most in forex: what was happening in the market in the seconds before this candle formed?

body.text: A candlestick pattern's shape is the same everywhere, but its reliability on forex depends heavily on when in the session cycle it formed. The identical hammer, doji or engulfing candle can mean genuine reversal or meaningless liquidity noise, depending on whether it formed at a session open, inside a quiet window, or during an overlap.

children.text: A quick reminder before the forex-specific part. Every candle plots four numbers for its period: the open, the high, the low and the close. The body is the range between open and close. The wicks, also called shadows, show how far price travelled beyond the body before pulling back. That part is identical to reading a candle on Nifty or Reliance. What changes in forex is what is happening on the other side of that candle, invisible on the chart itself.

markDefs.definition: A brief price spike right at a session open or major news release that triggers resting stop-loss and pending orders just beyond a round number or prior high or low, then reverses once genuine two-way liquidity returns.

children.text: In the first few minutes after any session opens, whether that is NSE's currency segment at 9:00 am IST or the London session at 12:30 pm IST, liquidity is thin and one-sided for a short burst. Orders that were resting overnight, including stop-losses parked just beyond an obvious round number like ₹95.00, all try to execute at once. This produces a

, a wick that pokes past a level and then snaps back once real depth arrives. It looks exactly like a textbook hammer or shooting star, but it was manufactured by thin liquidity, not by a genuine shift in buyers and sellers.

body.title: Illustrative USD/INR, First 10 Minutes After the 9:00 am NSE Open

children.text: This is an illustrative pattern, not a live quote. The 9:00 am candle pokes up to 95.52 and closes back near its open, which by itself looks like a bearish rejection wick. But notice what happens next: price does not reverse upward, it keeps drifting lower over the following ten minutes. The wick was the market clearing out stray buy orders left over from before the open, not a genuine signal that sellers had taken control. If Rohit had waited for the next one or two candles to confirm direction instead of trading the wick itself, he would have avoided the false signal.

body.text: The fix is not to ignore session-open wicks, it is to wait for confirmation. A hammer or shooting star at a session open becomes far more trustworthy once the next one or two candles hold in the implied direction, showing that real participants, not just leftover orders, are backing the move.

body.title: Wick or reversal?
body.question: A long lower wick forms on the very first candle after NSE's currency segment opens at 9:00 am. What should you do before treating it as a bullish reversal signal?
options: Buy immediately, since a hammer at the open is always reliable
Ignore it completely, since session-open candles are never useful
Wait for the next one or two candles to confirm price is actually holding higher
Check the RSI on the weekly chart before deciding
body.explanation: Session-open wicks are often liquidity grabs from resting orders rather than genuine reversals. Waiting for the following candles to confirm the direction filters out most of the false signals without discarding the pattern entirely.

children.text: Doji Candles: Indecision, or Just a Quiet Hour?

A doji, where the open and close sit almost on top of each other, is usually taught as a sign of indecision between buyers and sellers. On a stock chart, where every candle forms under roughly similar liquidity conditions, that reading holds up well. On forex, you first have to ask a simpler question: was there enough activity for indecision to even be meaningful?

body.title: The same doji shape, two very different meanings

columns.label: Doji at 3:00 am IST
points: Forms during the Sydney-only window, the thinnest liquidity of the day
Open and close are near identical simply because almost nothing happened
Carries little forecasting value on its own

columns.label: Doji at 7:00 pm IST
points: Forms during the London-New York overlap, the busiest window of the day
Open and close near identical despite heavy two-way activity
A genuinely meaningful tug of war between real buyers and sellers

body.title: The doji that meant nothing
body.scenario: Meera spots a doji on the EUR/USD hourly chart at 3:30 am IST, right after a small dip and recovery. She has read that a doji after a decline often signals a reversal, so she goes long, expecting a bounce. The trade drifts sideways for hours and eventually stops her out on a small pullback with no real move in either direction.
body.prompt: Using what you now know about liquidity and session timing, explain why this doji was a weak signal, and what time of day would have made the identical candle shape more meaningful.
body.modelAnswer:
1. 3:30 am IST falls in the Sydney-only window, the thinnest liquidity period of the day, so a doji here often just means very little trading happened, not that buyers and sellers fought to a standstill.
2. With few participants active, the open and close landing close together is close to the default outcome, so it carries little forecasting value.
3. The identical doji shape would be far more meaningful during the London-New York overlap, roughly 5:30 pm to 9:30 pm IST, where heavy two-way volume genuinely fighting to a draw is a real signal.
4. Meera should treat low-liquidity-window candlestick patterns as low-confidence by default, and reserve full-size trades for patterns confirmed during active sessions.

children.text: Pin Bars and Engulfing Patterns: Reading Session Backing

body.caption: Two patterns you will use constantly on currency charts

cells: A small body with one long wick, at least twice the body length, pointing away from the recent trend
Price pushed hard in one direction and got firmly rejected
A candle whose body fully covers the entire body of the candle before it, in the opposite colour
A sharp shift in control from sellers to buyers, or buyers to sellers

children.text: The forex-specific catch with engulfing patterns is that a session transition can manufacture a convincing-looking engulfing candle out of nothing more than the arrival of liquidity. A tiny, near-flat candle formed in a quiet window, followed immediately by a large candle the moment a major session opens, will satisfy the textbook definition of engulfing almost automatically, because the first candle was artificially small to begin with.

body.title: Illustrative EUR/USD, Tokyo Quiet Period Into the London Open

body.text: This is an illustrative pattern, not a live quote, but the trap is real. The tiny 12:00 pm candle is not evidence of a genuine standoff between buyers and sellers, it is simply what candles look like right before London wakes up. The large 12:30 pm candle engulfing it may still be a valid bullish signal, but you should credit that to London's arriving volume, not to some meaningful battle that was won in the prior candle.

body.title: Naming the trap
body.textWithBlank: An engulfing pattern that forms only because a tiny candle from a quiet window is followed by a large candle as a new session opens should be credited to the arrival of ___, not to a genuine standoff between buyers and sellers in the earlier candle.
body.explanation: The size difference between the two candles often has more to do with which session was active than with any real shift in buying and selling pressure.

children.text: The Opening Candle's Gap on NSE Currency Futures

One more forex-specific quirk worth flagging here, though Chapter 3 covers gap trading properly. Because NSE's currency segment is closed from 5:00 pm to 9:00 am IST while global spot EUR/USD, GBP/USD and the dollar index keep moving overnight, USD/INR futures routinely open with a gap from the previous day's close, the same way Nifty gaps up or down based on overnight cues from US markets. A large overnight move in the dollar or a surprise US Federal Reserve statement can show up as a clean gap on the very first candle of the NSE session.

body.title: Sizing the gap
body.prompt: USD/INR futures closed at ₹95.20 on Thursday. Overnight, the US dollar strengthens broadly. On Friday, NSE's currency segment opens at ₹95.68. How large is the opening gap, in paise?
body.explanation: 95.68 minus 95.20 equals 0.48, or 48 paise. A gap this size on the opening candle is a genuine signal worth noting, since it is an actual exchange price jump, not a liquidity artifact like the wicks discussed earlier in this lesson.

body.title: Candlestick Reading on Forex: Key Terms

cards.definition: A brief price spike right at a session open or news release that triggers resting orders just beyond a round number, then reverses once real two-way liquidity returns.
A candle with a small body and one long wick, at least twice the body length, showing a firm rejection of price in the wick's direction.
A candle whose body fully covers the entire body of the previous candle in the opposite colour, signalling a sharp shift in control.
A candle where the open and close are nearly identical. Meaningful mainly when it forms during a period of genuine two-way activity.
The difference between NSE currency futures' previous close and the next day's open, driven by overnight moves in global spot forex.

points: A candle's shape reads the same on every chart, but its reliability on forex depends heavily on when in the session cycle it formed.
Session-open wicks are often liquidity grabs from resting orders, not genuine reversals. Wait for the next candle or two to confirm direction before trusting one.

A doji formed in the thin Sydney-only window, roughly 2:30 am to 5:30 am IST, is a weak signal. The identical doji during the London-New York overlap, roughly 5:30 pm to 9:30 pm IST, is far more meaningful.
Engulfing patterns that span a session transition can be manufactured by the arrival of liquidity rather than a genuine standoff between buyers and sellers in the smaller candle.
USD/INR futures on NSE regularly gap on the opening candle because global spot forex keeps moving while the exchange is closed overnight. Chapter 3 covers gap-based patterns in full.
The general rule across all of these: treat a pattern's confidence as tied to the session it formed in, not just its shape.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not trading advice. The candlestick examples throughout are illustrative and not live or historical quotes. Candlestick patterns are probabilistic tools, not guarantees, and should be combined with the liquidity and session context from earlier lessons, proper risk management and your own analysis before any trade.
